content: Cephalanthus occidentalis, commonly known as Buttonbush, Button-bush, Button-willow, or Honey-bells, is a plant species native to the eastern and southern regions of North America. It is a deciduous shrub or small tree that typically grows to a height of 2 to 10 meters, although in rare cases, it can reach up to 15 meters. The leaves of Cephalanthus occidentalis are arranged either oppositely or in whorls of three. They are elliptic to ovate in shape, measuring between 7 and 20 centimeters in length and 3 to 7 centimeters in width. The leaf margins are smooth (entire), and the leaves are attached to the stem by short petioles. The flowers are borne on peduncles that are approximately 5 centimeters long. Each individual flower features a fused corolla that is white to pale yellow in color and has four lobes. The corolla forms a long, slender tube that connects to the calyx. The stigma of the flower is elongated and protrudes about 4 millimeters beyond the corolla. There are two recognized varieties of Cephalanthus occidentalis, though not all authorities consider them to be distinct: 1. Cephalanthus occidentalis var. occidentalis (synonym: var. pubescens), commonly referred to as the Common Buttonbush, is found in eastern North America. Its range extends from Nova Scotia westward to Minnesota and southward to Florida and eastern Texas. 2. Cephalanthus occidentalis var. californicus, known as the California Button-willow, is native to southwestern North America. Its distribution includes western Texas, California (such as the Sierra Nevada foothills, San Joaquin Valley, Sacramento Valley, and the Inner North Coast Ranges), and extends southward into Mexico and Central America.
